The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. It states that every non-constant polynomial of degree n with complex coefficients has exactly n roots in the complex numbers, counting multiplicity. This theorem completes the number system by guaranteeing that polynomial equations always have solutions within the complex field, no matter their degree. Carl Friedrich Gauss gave the first rigorous proof in seventeen ninety-nine, and the result is foundational to all of algebra, analysis, and applied mathematics.

If p of x is a polynomial of degree n greater than or equal to one with complex coefficients, then there exist exactly n complex numbers r one, r two, through r n, not necessarily distinct, such that p of x factors as a n times the product of x minus r i. Here a n is the leading coefficient. Repeated roots are counted according to their multiplicity. A root that appears k times in the factorization has multiplicity k.

A polynomial with real coefficients may have complex roots, but they occur in conjugate pairs. If a plus b i is a root, then a minus b i is also a root. This ensures real factorization structure. The theorem guarantees the existence of roots but does not provide a method to find them. For degree greater than or equal to five, no closed-form radical solution exists, according to Galois theory.

Historically, earlier centuries saw solutions for low-degree polynomials. Cardano solved cubics, Ferrari solved quartics, but the general case eluded proof until Gauss's rigorous argument in seventeen ninety-nine. The set of real numbers is not algebraically closed. The polynomial x squared plus one has no real roots, which is why complex numbers were necessary. Every polynomial can be uniquely factored into linear factors in the complex numbers. This factorization is the starting point for partial fractions, residue calculus, and signal processing.

Gauss's original proof was geometric. Later proofs use complex analysis through the argument principle, topology through winding number arguments, or algebra through reduction to the case of real polynomials via conjugation.
